summary:
Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationally and reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch, in its October 2016 report on the act, found that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and documented police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria, reported in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, restates the exposure to up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity and identifies a death-penalty risk under Sharia law in the northern states.

Reporting on the tenth year of the act (Context, August 2024) describes the law as having fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and as effectively sanctioning abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and an increase in attacks since it passed. The 2014 act is described in the same coverage and elsewhere as reinforcing criminalisation inherited from the colonial period rather than introducing it.

Enforcement is documented as violent and predatory. A 24-year-old man stopped by police in Lagos was struck in the mouth with the butt of a police gun and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, the officers' stated reason being that he 'looked gay' (TimesLIVE, March 2025). People affected by the law describe it as weaponised and as having created a climate of hostility.

Raids on private gatherings and hotels have produced mass arrests. More than 100 people attending a party at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, were arrested in June 2018; 57 young men were arrested at a hotel in Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; 67 people were arrested in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe State in October 2023. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011.

A documented killing of a transgender woman remains unprosecuted. The beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman known as Abuja Area Mama, who had a social-media following, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend. The police account described the victim as 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police commissioner ordered a thorough and discreet investigation; six months later no suspect had been charged (The Dial, February 2025). The same reporting notes that Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the police response to the killing is documented as having produced no arrests.

Custody practice for transgender women is discretionary. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024 to four counts of abuse of the naira currency and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing (BBC Pidgin) asked publicly which prison 'they will keep the crossdresser in', an indication that placement is decided case by case, and the available account does not record whether she was held in a male or a female section. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that her placement in a maximum-security prison breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Dating applications are used as traps. 'Kito' gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed under threat of being outed; community members have responded with exposure forums, including one administrator's alert page with 43,000 followers, and with sting operations against the gangs (Context, April 2024). A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications is exposed to the same luring and blackmail pattern, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.

Proposals to criminalise cross-dressing have been reported and were met with fear among transgender Nigerians (Reuters, September 2022). Many LGBTQ+ Nigerians also fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes to the police because of arrest and 'kito' extortion risk.
tangentialFactors: The Federal Ministry of Education operates a national policy on safety, security and violence-free schools covering all Nigerian schools, which prohibits discrimination explicitly including on the ground of 'sexual orientation', even though no enacted legislation protects against discrimination generally and no political party endorses LGBTQ+ rights. Section 17(3)(d) of the Nigerian Constitution nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens, a guarantee that sits alongside the criminalisation regime rather than displacing it.
localsOnly:
Residents report loss of employment and livelihoods following the 2014 act. Activists say the law hampers access to HIV prevention services and has forced LGBTQ+ people and their allies to abandon community health and education work. A 2015 survey by Bisi Alimi's organisation found that only 30 per cent of Nigerians agreed that LGBTQ+ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing.

Religious institutions play a central role in education, and mainstream interpretations of Islam and Christianity drive the stigmatisation of LGBTQ+ students. The House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after its members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008, and some members were then threatened, beaten and stoned. Two non-governmental organisations, Global Rights and The Independent Project, provided LGBT groups with HIV/AIDS awareness training, according to a US State Department report from 2011.
outOfScopeNotes: Whether any of the reported proposals to criminalise cross-dressing were enacted is not established by the sources surveyed. The account of the 2024 custody case does not record whether the prisoner was assigned to a male or female section, so placement can be described as discretionary while its typical result cannot. No published figures for prosecutions or convictions under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 were located, so the frequency of enforcement against any individual cannot be quantified. The August 2026 travel warning is reported through a Nigerian news outlet rather than retrieved from the issuing government's own publication. The disposition of the men arrested in Bauchi in 2007 after their case lapsed at the end of 2011 is not recorded.
